The paper presents a computational approach that combines crystal plasticity (CP) and extended finite element method (XFEM) to model short crack propagation in a single crystal nickel-based superalloy.
The onset of fracture is controlled by the cumulative shear strain of individual slip systems, and the direction of crack growth follows the crystallographic slip plane.
Simulations were carried out for the [111] orientation at 24°C and 650°C.
The critical value of the individual cumulative shear strain (ICSS) was chosen as 0.026 for 24°C and 0.020 for 650°C based on observations from the simulations.
The CP model parameters were calibrated using low-cycle fatigue (LCF) experimental data at 24°C and 825°C, and then linearly interpolated to obtain the parameters for 650°C.
The simulations were able to predict the tortuous crack path and irregular propagation rate, which are characteristics of short crack growth in single crystal nickel-based superalloys.
The authors introduced manual control to handle the XFEM limitations of only allowing a single straight crack per element and crack deflection greater than 90 degrees.
A 2D plane strain model was used instead of a 3D model to facilitate the extremely time-consuming CP-XFEM simulations under fatigue loading conditions.
The in-situ SEM experiments were conducted at room temperature (24°C) and 650°C, while the LCF tests used for CP model calibration were performed at 24°C and 825°C.

The authors found that the crack growth path predicted by the two mesh densities (average element size of ~2.5 μm and ~1.25 μm) followed almost the same path, indicating a relatively small effect of the manual control process on the overall crack path.

The energy-based exponential function used to describe the damage evolution of XFEM elements had an exponent of 2 and a dissipated energy of 0.001 to ensure fast but numerically stable element damage.
The maximum time increment was set as 0.01 second to avoid numerical instability and reduce the influence of partially damaged elements.
The deviations of maximum stress level between experiments and simulations were less than 30 MPa at both 24°C and 825°C conditions.
The deviations of maximum and minimum stress between experiments and simulations were less than 90 MPa at both 24°C and 825°C conditions.

The interpolation of CP model parameters from 24°C and 825°C to 650°C can introduce some inaccuracies for the strain-stress behaviour, but it is not expected to significantly affect the ICSS distribution at the crack tip.
